drafted_from: tool:set-up-a-servers-tls-owner's row in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/tool-rows.json, do-work/renew-a-tls-certificate.mjs, do-work/tls-host-owner.py and the tests in test/
start_here: Say to your AI: "Set up the certificate owner on my server at 192.0.2.34 for app.example.com, reached as admin with its pinned key." It runs tool:set-up-a-servers-tls-owner: owner, layout, certbot, nginx and the receptionist account, with no traffic change.
no_lists_because: It keeps no list of its own: it takes one server's facts as its input and answers what that server's certificate owner reports.
instructions: 1. Gather the server's facts: its public name, IPv4 address, SSH port, the administrator you sign in as, its pinned key ("<address> ssh-ed25519 <key>") and its layout (host: owner path, state folder, downloads folder, ingress, receptionist). The README in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/ shows a made-up one.

2. Say to your AI the sentence in start_here. It calls run_resource_operation at @workshop-tools with method tools:run, tool tool:set-up-a-servers-tls-owner and that input (the worked example shows one). The door mounts your server administration key for the run; you paste no key.

3. Read what comes back: {"packages_installed": true, "default_http_not_enabled": true, "dns_credentials_on_disk": false}. An {"error": ...} or a thrown message names what to change (for example the layout or the pinned key was refused).
4. Next run tool:issue-a-tls-certificate, then tool:write-a-public-hosts-paths. If only the owner or its layout changes later, use tool:update-a-servers-tls-owner.
